title: Grade Rescue — daily rotation
source: Carter's Ch 13 guide: her slide deck 1-51 plus his spoken priority list; bio items 1-21 cover the starred meiosis/Mendel/Hardy-Weinberg scope for the 11/13 quiz

questions.stem: A human karyotype is prepared from a somatic cell and the chromosomes are arranged in 23 pairs. How many of those pairs are autosomes, and what does the pairing itself show?
options: 22 autosome pairs; the members of each pair are homologs, matched in length and shape, one from each parent.
23 autosome pairs; the pairing shows the cell is haploid.
22 autosome pairs; each pair is a set of sister chromatids made in S phase.
46 autosome pairs; each pair represents a separate chromosome set.
questions.why: Humans have 22 autosome pairs plus one sex-chromosome pair, and homologs match in length and shape with one copy from each parent.

questions.stem: A city council candidate opens a speech: "I have met a payroll for twenty years. I know what a dollar buys." Which appeal is primary, and on what does it rest?
options: Pathos, resting on the audience's fear of unemployment.
Ethos, resting on the speaker's credibility and experience.
Logos, resting on a statistical comparison of budgets.
Kairos, resting on the urgency of the current election.
questions.why: The speaker offers no data and no emotional scene; the claim to authority is the credential itself, which is ethos.

questions.stem: A sperm cell carries a Y chromosome. What does that tell you about the zygote it will form, and about the sperm's own chromosome set?
options: The zygote will be XX and female, and the sperm was diploid.
The zygote will be XY and male, and the sperm carried two sets of 23.
The zygote will be XY and male, and the sperm carried one set of 23, so it was haploid.
The zygote's sex cannot be predicted because the egg may also carry a Y.
questions.why: An unfertilized egg always carries X, so a Y-bearing sperm gives XY, a male; gametes carry a single set, so the sperm is haploid (n = 23).

questions.stem: Draft thesis: "Homework is bad." Which revision would most strengthen it for an AP argument essay?
options: Homework should be abolished everywhere immediately.
Homework is bad for students in many ways.
Homework: some say it helps, some say it hurts.
Schools should cap nightly homework at 45 minutes per subject, because the sleep it costs outweighs the marginal practice it buys.
questions.why: The revision names a specific policy, a reason, and a measurable cost, so a reader can agree or disagree with it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly pairs meiosis with fertilization in a human life cycle?
options: Meiosis produces haploid gametes (n = 23), and fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46).
Meiosis doubles the chromosome number, and fertilization halves it.
Both meiosis and fertilization produce haploid cells, and mitosis restores 46.
Meiosis produces diploid gametes, and fertilization reduces them to 23.
questions.why: Meiosis halves the set to n in gametes; fusion of two n gametes gives 2n = 46 in the zygote.

questions.stem: An essay argues that later school start times improve attendance. Which sentence best concedes a real objection?
options: Anyone who opposes later start times is ignoring the science.
Critics point out that bus schedules are hard to change, but the districts that shifted pickup times still saw attendance gains.
Attendance is the only outcome that matters here.
Later start times are obviously better for every student.
questions.why: It grants the strongest practical objection and answers it with evidence, which is what a concession must do to earn credit.

questions.stem: During prophase I a segment of one nonsister chromatid is exchanged with the corresponding segment of the other. Which outcome follows, and in which phase does it happen?
options: The chromosome number drops from 46 to 23, in prophase I.
The two sister chromatids become identical again, in metaphase I.
The recombinant chromatids carry new combinations of alleles, and it happens in prophase I.
Homologs are pulled to opposite poles, in anaphase I.
questions.why: Crossing over swaps corresponding segments between nonsister chromatids in prophase I, so each chromatid ends up with a mixed set of alleles.

questions.stem: A student claims a new tutoring program raised scores. Which evidence would most directly support that claim?
options: Anecdotes from two students who enjoyed the tutors.
The district's rising graduation rate over the past ten years.
The program's cost per student compared with other districts.
A before-and-after comparison of the same students' scores set against a matched group that did not enroll.
questions.why: A comparison with a matched non-enrolled group controls for other causes, which is what makes the claim about the program testable.

questions.stem: Two homologous pairs (Aa and Bb) orient at the metaphase I plate. What does independent assortment predict about the gametes?
options: Gametes include AB, Ab, aB and ab, because each pair orients independently of the other.
All gametes carry either AB or ab, because the pairs travel together.
Gametes carry two copies of each gene, because the pairs have not separated.
Only two gamete types form, because crossing over fixes the combinations.
questions.why: Each pair lines up without reference to the others, so the two orientations combine to give four equally likely gamete types.

questions.stem: A report lists eleven failed inspections in one sentence, then closes the paragraph with four words: "The building passed." What does that final sentence do?
options: It supplies the statistical summary the list lacked.
It delivers the outcome with no transition, so the flat close undercuts the list and creates irony.
It concedes that the list of failures was exaggerated.
It restates the list's main point in simpler words.
questions.why: The abrupt, unqualified verdict after eleven failures is an ironic juxtaposition; the effect depends on the absence of a transition.

questions.stem: Four gametes from a single 2n = 8 cell carry 5, 5, 3 and 3 chromosomes. Crossing over was normal. Which division failed?
options: Meiosis II, because only one of the two cells divided badly.
Crossing over, because it changed the chromosome count.
Meiosis I, because every gamete is abnormal and the error is in homolog separation.
Cytokinesis, because it failed after meiosis II.
questions.why: When both products of meiosis I carry the error, all four gametes are abnormal — two with an extra chromosome and two missing one, offsetting 4 each.

questions.stem: A memo describes a 300 percent budget overrun as "a modest variance." What does the understatement accomplish?
options: It exaggerates the size of the overrun for emphasis.
It shifts responsibility for the overrun to the auditors.
It gives the reader a precise measurement of the overrun.
It makes the overrun sound routine by naming it blandly, which is the ironic effect.
questions.why: Understatement deliberately under-names a large problem; the gap between the word and the fact is the irony.

questions.stem: A cell is observed in anaphase II. Which description matches that stage?
options: Sister chromatids have separated and are moving to opposite poles as individual chromosomes.
Homologous chromosomes are being pulled to opposite poles, each still two chromatids.
Homologs have paired and are exchanging corresponding segments.
A nucleus is re-forming around 46 chromosomes.
questions.why: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so each chromatid becomes its own chromosome moving to a pole.

questions.stem: "The policy was a paper umbrella in a hurricane." What does the metaphor imply about the policy?
options: It was expensive but broadly popular.
It offered protection that could not possibly hold up under the pressure it faced.
It caused the storm of criticism that followed.
It was written by officials who never saw a storm.
questions.why: A paper umbrella looks like protection and fails instantly in a hurricane, so the vehicle carries uselessness under real stress.

questions.stem: Which set correctly names the three mechanisms that produce genetic variation among offspring, and states the combination formula for independent assortment?
options: Mutation, mitosis and fertilization; 2n combinations, where n is the diploid number.
Crossing over, cytokinesis and nondisjunction; n^2 combinations.
Independent assortment, crossing over and random fertilization; 2^n combinations, where n is the haploid number.
Independent assortment, translation and fertilization; 2^n combinations.
questions.why: Her three sources are independent assortment, crossing over and random fertilization; chromosomes assorting independently give 2^n gamete combinations.

questions.stem: "The committee met. It debated. It adjourned. Nothing changed." What does the run of short sentences accomplish?
options: It creates a sense of exhaustive detail about the meeting.
It establishes the committee's authority on the issue.
It softens the criticism of how the committee worked.
It mirrors the stalemate by flattening four events into equal, unconnected beats.
questions.why: Equal, clipped sentences with no subordination make the events feel weightless, which is the point about the outcome.

questions.stem: At anaphase I, what separates and what stays together?
options: Homologous chromosomes separate, and sister chromatids stay attached at the centromere.
Sister chromatids separate, and homologs stay paired at the plate.
Homologs and sister chromatids separate at the same moment.
Nothing separates, and the cell divides with 46 duplicated chromosomes.
questions.why: Anaphase I pulls homologs apart while cohesin along the arms is cut; centromeric cohesin persists so sisters travel as one unit.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a claim that is best qualified for an AP argument essay?
options: Standardized tests are useless.
Standardized tests tend to reward test-taking skill as much as content knowledge, especially for students without coaching.
Everyone knows standardized tests are unfair.
Standardized tests should be abolished by Friday.
questions.why: A hedged, conditional claim with a named exception leaves room for evidence, which an absolute claim does not.

questions.stem: A round-seeded plant is crossed with a wrinkled-seeded plant (rr), and all 60 offspring are round. What does that result establish about the round-seeded parent?
options: It is heterozygous (Rr), because half the offspring should be wrinkled.
It proves seed shape and height are linked genes.
It is homozygous dominant (RR), because no recessive offspring appeared among 60.
Nothing can be concluded without a second cross to the same parent.
questions.why: A heterozygote crossed to rr yields about 1:1; with 60 offspring all dominant, the parent is almost certainly RR — the absence of the recessive class is the evidence.

questions.stem: "Either we restore the arts budget or we admit we do not care about children." Which flaw is present?
options: Ad hominem, because it attacks a person rather than a claim.
Slippery slope, because it predicts a chain of disasters.
Straw man, because it misstates an opponent's position.
False dilemma, because only two options are offered where more exist.
questions.why: The sentence forces a choice between two extremes and ignores every middle option, which is the false dilemma.

questions.stem: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9 percent of individuals show the recessive phenotype. What fraction of the population is heterozygous?
options: 0.42, because q = 0.3 and 2pq = 0.42.
0.09, because the recessive phenotype count equals the heterozygote count.
0.21, because q multiplied by p gives the heterozygote fraction.
0.49, because p squared gives the heterozygote fraction.

questions.stem: An op-ed opens: "Who decided that a fifteen-minute passing period was enough for two thousand students?" What does the question do for the argument?
options: It supplies evidence about how the schedule was built.
It frames the schedule as an unreasonable decision the reader is invited to question.
It concedes that fifteen minutes is adequate.
It shifts the argument to an unrelated topic.
questions.why: A rhetorical question presupposes its answer, so the reader accepts the premise that the decision was arbitrary.

questions.stem: A drug inhibits DNA ligase in a replicating cell. Which consequence appears on the lagging strand?
options: Helicase can no longer unwind the double helix.
Primase can no longer lay down RNA primers.
Okazaki fragments remain unjoined, leaving nicks in the new strand.
The leading strand is synthesized in the wrong direction.
questions.why: Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments; without it the fragments stay separate even though synthesis itself proceeds.

questions.stem: "We asked for the data. We asked for a timeline. We asked for a plan." What is the effect of the repeated opening?
options: It suggests the requests were all satisfied in turn.
It introduces three unrelated claims.
It weakens the paragraph through unnecessary repetition.
It builds insistence and implies the requests went unanswered.
questions.why: Anaphora accumulates pressure; three identical requests imply refusal, not completion.

questions.stem: A single base is inserted early in a coding region. What is the most likely consequence for the protein?
options: Every codon downstream is read in a shifted frame, so the protein is usually nonfunctional.
One amino acid is substituted and the rest of the protein is unchanged.
Transcription stops immediately at the point of insertion.
The mRNA is degraded before translation can begin.
questions.why: An insertion shifts the reading frame, changing every downstream codon and usually producing a truncated or garbled protein.

questions.stem: An essay on school funding opens with the writer's memory of a leaking classroom ceiling. What is the main risk of that opening?
options: It cannot support any argument about funding.
It can read as sentimental and delay the argument unless it is quickly tied to a claim.
It makes the essay too statistical for a general reader.
It assumes the reader already agrees with the writer.
questions.why: A personal scene earns attention but costs time; its value depends on how fast the writer converts it into a claim.

questions.stem: In the lac operon, glucose is absent and lactose is present. Which pairing correctly describes the two regulator proteins?
options: CAP is bound and the repressor is bound, so transcription is off.
CAP is released and the repressor is bound, so transcription is off.
CAP is bound and the repressor is released, so transcription is high.
CAP is released and the repressor is released, so transcription is low.
questions.why: Low glucose raises cAMP so CAP binds and activates; lactose removes the repressor, so both conditions favor high expression.

questions.stem: A health department flyer states that 340 residents waited more than six hours for care last year. Which appeal does the specific number chiefly serve?
options: Ethos, because the department is an authority.
Logos only, because numbers cannot move an audience.
None, because statistics are neutral by definition.
Pathos, because the concrete number makes the burden on real people immediate.
questions.why: The number is used for its human weight rather than its proof value, so it functions as an emotional appeal in context.

questions.stem: A gene is inserted into a plasmid in the middle of an ampicillin-resistance gene, disrupting it. What should be true of bacteria carrying the recombinant plasmid?
options: They are sensitive to ampicillin but can still grow on plates without it.
They are resistant to ampicillin and grow on any plate.
They are resistant to ampicillin and to a second antibiotic.
They cannot replicate the plasmid at all.
questions.why: Insertional inactivation removes resistance, so recombinants lose the ability to grow on ampicillin while remaining viable without it.

questions.stem: How would combining one long periodic sentence with several short declaratives most likely affect a paragraph?
options: Every sentence would carry equal weight and emphasis.
The long sentence would carry the qualification while the short ones deliver the verdict.
The paragraph would no longer need evidence.
The paragraph would become harder to follow in every case.
questions.why: Varying length assigns roles: the suspended clause holds complexity, and the clipped sentence lands the judgment.

questions.stem: On an island, a lizard population has larger jaws in years when only hard seeds are available. Which statement explains this as natural selection rather than individual change?
options: Individual lizards grew larger jaws by eating hard seeds.
The hard seeds caused new jaw mutations in the population.
Lizards with larger jaws survived and reproduced more in hard-seed years, so those alleles increased.
Jaw size is not heritable, so selection cannot act on it.
questions.why: Selection changes allele frequencies across generations through differential reproduction, not through an individual's use or disuse.

questions.stem: "If we install lights, more students will play sports, so grades will rise, so the dropout rate will fall." What is the main weakness?
options: The first claim is irrelevant to the conclusion.
The conclusion contradicts the premises.
The argument relies on a false dilemma.
Each link is asserted rather than shown, so the chain needs evidence at every step.
questions.why: A causal chain is only as strong as its weakest link; here every transition is assumed, so the reasoning is unsupported at three points.

questions.stem: A fertilizer trial measures yield in one treated field and one untreated field. Which change would most strengthen the design?
options: Replicate each treatment across several fields and assign treatments at random.
Measure the treated field more often than the untreated field.
Use a larger field for the treated condition.
Drop the untreated field to save time and money.
questions.why: Replication and random assignment control for field-to-field variation and for confounding, which a single pair of fields cannot.
